title: Capstone: URL shortener
summary: Run the whole frame on one small system without new mechanisms.

body:
Rule. Assemble the prior system-design lessons on one product: requirements, estimates, API, data model, read/write paths, cache, failure. Do not invent a brand-new mechanism this track never taught. Prefer the simplest store that meets the access paths. Deep-dive one bottleneck such as code generation or cache correctness.

Why it matters. Capstones test integration, not novelty. Candidates who suddenly invent CRDTs or multi-region consensus for a shortener show panic, not mastery. Reusing the frame cleanly is the point.

Worked example. Requirements: create link, redirect, optional delete; park analytics. Estimate: forty writes/sec, four hundred reads/sec, tens of GB storage. API: POST /v1/links, GET /{code}, DELETE /v1/links/{code}. Model: links(code PK, url, owner_id, created_at). Write path inserts; read path PK get with cache keyed by code and delete-on-update invalidation. Code generation: draw random seven-char codes, INSERT, retry on primary-key conflict — expected retries tiny. Failure: redirect path times out cache at 50 ms then hits SQL; create path retries conflict three times then errors. Replicas optional at this QPS; sharding not required yet. You reused estimates, paths, cache, and failure without adding a stream processor. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism.

[[diagram:shorten]]

When to use. Use as a rehearsal for interview pacing. Use it to practice saying no to unnecessary components. Use the deep dive to show judgment on one sharp problem.

When to refuse. Refuse adding Kafka, multi-region, or ML-based codes without a requirement that needs them. Refuse skipping estimates because the product "seems small." Refuse a design with no failure story on redirect. Refuse treating the capstone as a license to introduce untaught machinery.
